claims.text: An active-learning framework coupling machine-learned interatomic potentials with reversible thermodynamic integration can dramatically reduce the cost of calculating fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The proposed framework can faithfully retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling in both solid and liquid states.
The method is intended for elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys near fusion conditions.
The machine-learned potential will be iteratively trained on ab initio configurations spanning both solid and fluid phases.
A reversible integration path will compute phase free-energy differences while accurately accounting for critical entropy contributions.
The framework is applicable below, at, and above the melting point.
The framework is applicable from elemental and binary systems through complex multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Machine-learned potentials can represent atomic interactions with fidelity comparable to ab initio methods while drastically reducing computational cost.
Active learning identifies and fills training-set gaps, particularly in regions exhibiting strong anharmonic or electron–vibration effects.
Filling those training-set gaps ensures accurate reproduction of the free-energy landscapes of both solid and liquid phases.
Thermodynamic integration along a reversible path captures vibrational, anharmonic, and electronic entropy contributions.
Phase free energies, melting temperature, and latent heat will agree with explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results to within approximately 5%.
The proposed method will execute orders of magnitude faster than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will be considerably faster than TOR-TILD, especially for multicomponent systems.
First-principles workflows are computationally demanding for multi-principal-element alloys.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluations are accurate but computationally expensive.
TOR-TILD calculations are especially computationally expensive for multicomponent and high-entropy systems.
Vibrational entropy is thermodynamically relevant to stabilization in a multicomponent CoCrFeNi-Ta alloy system.
Training-set incompleteness may limit treatment of extreme anharmonic and electron–vibration effects in complex or under-sampled regions.
A discrepancy greater than approximately 5% in phase free energies or derived thermodynamic observables relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics would falsify the hypothesis.
